lesson.title: Encoding: Turning Bits into a Physical Signal
lesson.summary: Encoding is the process of translating a digital bit stream into the actual voltage levels, light pulses, or other physical signal changes that a medium can carry, and the choices made here shape everything from timing recovery to noise resistance.
lesson.body:
A digital signal, as a concept, is an abstraction: a sequence of discrete values, ones and zeros, that a computer works with internally. None of that abstraction moves through a wire or a fiber by itself. Before any bit stream can leave a network interface, it has to be translated into something physical, a pattern of voltage levels on a copper wire, pulses of light in a fiber, or changes in a radio signal, that a receiver on the other end can measure and interpret. That translation step, from abstract bits to concrete physical signal, is what encoding means at the physical layer.

The obvious first idea, just assign one voltage level to 1 and another to 0 and hold each level for one bit period, actually works, and you will see it formally in the next chapter under the name NRZ. But that obvious approach runs into real problems once you think about how a receiver actually reads a signal. A receiver has no built in sense of where one bit ends and the next begins; it needs a clock, and in most designs that clock is recovered from the incoming signal itself by watching for transitions. A long run of identical bits, all 1s or all 0s, produces a flat, unchanging signal with nothing for a clock recovery circuit to lock onto, so the receiver's sense of timing can drift and bits can be miscounted. A signal that sits at one DC level for a long stretch can also accumulate what is called baseline wander on transformer coupled or AC coupled lines, further degrading a receiver's ability to tell levels apart.

Good line encoding schemes are designed around these constraints. Engineers generally want a scheme to be self clocking, meaning it guarantees regular signal transitions regardless of the data pattern, so the receiver's clock never has long silences to drift during. They want it to be roughly DC balanced, meaning it spends about as much time at a high level as a low level over any stretch of data, avoiding baseline wander. They want it to make efficient use of available bandwidth, and ideally to have some built in ability to reveal transmission errors. No single scheme maximizes every one of these properties at once, which is exactly why several different encoding schemes exist and why network engineers pick among them based on the medium and the data rate involved.

The two schemes you will look at next, NRZ and Manchester encoding, sit at opposite ends of a real trade off. NRZ is bandwidth efficient but gives up self clocking, so it depends on other tricks or usage patterns to keep a receiver synchronized. Manchester encoding sacrifices bandwidth efficiency, needing roughly twice the signal bandwidth for the same bit rate, in exchange for a transition in every single bit period no matter what the data looks like. Once you have encoding straight as the general problem of mapping bits to a physical signal, the receiver's job of reversing that mapping, called decoding, is the natural next step, and the specific schemes that make both directions practical follow right after.
